In [[mathematics]] &mdash; specifically, in [[geometric measure theory]] &mdash; '''spherical measure''' ''&sigma;''<sup>''n''</sup> is the "natural" [[Borel measure]] on the [[n-sphere|''n''-sphere]] '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>.  Spherical measure is often normalized so that it is a [[probability measure]] on the sphere, i.e. so that ''&sigma;''<sup>''n''</sup>('''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>)&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.

==Definition of spherical measure==

There are several ways to define spherical measure.  One way is to use the usual "round" or "[[arclength]]" [[metric space|metric]] ''&rho;''<sub>''n''</sub> on '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>;  that is, for points ''x'' and ''y'' in '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>, ''&rho;''<sub>''n''</sub>(''x'',&nbsp;''y'') is defined to be the (Euclidean) angle that they subtend at the centre of the sphere (the origin of '''R'''<sup>''n''+1</sup>).  Now construct ''n''-dimensional [[Hausdorff measure]] ''H''<sup>''n''</sup> on the metric space ('''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>,&nbsp;''&rho;''<sub>''n''</sub>) and define
:<math>\sigma^{n} = \frac{1}{H^{n}(\mathbf{S}^{n})} H^{n}.</math>
One could also have given '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup> the metric that it inherits as a subspace of the Euclidean space '''R'''<sup>''n''+1</sup>;  the same spherical measure results from this choice of metric.

Another method uses [[Lebesgue measure]] ''&lambda;''<sup>''n''+1</sup> on the ambient Euclidean space '''R'''<sup>''n''+1</sup>:  for any measurable subset ''A'' of '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>, define ''&sigma;''<sup>''n''</sup>(''A'') to be the (''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)-dimensional volume of the "wedge" in the ball '''B'''<sup>''n''+1</sup> that it subtends at the origin.  That is,
:<math>\sigma^{n}(A) := \frac{1}{\alpha(n + 1)} \lambda^{n + 1} ( \{ t x \mid x \in A, t \in [0, 1] \} ),</math>
where
:<math>\alpha(m) := \lambda^{m} (\mathbf{B}_{1}^{m} (0)) \text{ } (\mathbf{B}_1^{m} (0) \text{ is the ball of radius 1 centered at the origin in } </math>'''R'''<sup>''n''+1</sup>). 

The fact that all these methods define the same measure on '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup> follows from an elegant result of Christensen:  all these measures are obviously [[uniformly distributed measure|uniformly distributed]] on '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>, and any two uniformly distributed Borel regular measures on a separable metric space must be constant (positive) multiples of one another.  Since all our candidate ''&sigma;''<sup>''n''</sup>'s have been normalized to be probability measures, they are all the same measure.

==Relationship with other measures==

The relationship of spherical measure to Hausdorff measure on the sphere and Lebesgue measure on the ambient space has already been discussed.

Spherical measure has a nice relationship to [[Haar measure]] on the [[orthogonal group]].  Let O(''n'') denote the orthogonal group [[Group action (mathematics)|acting]] on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and let ''&theta;''<sup>''n''</sup> denote its normalized Haar measure (so that ''&theta;''<sup>''n''</sup>(O(''n''))&nbsp;=&nbsp;1).  The orthogonal group also acts on the sphere '''S'''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup>.  Then, for any ''x''&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;'''S'''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup> and any ''A''&nbsp;&sube;&nbsp;'''S'''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup>,
:<math>\theta^{n}(\{ g \in \mathrm{O}(n) \mid g(x) \in A \}) = \sigma^{n - 1}(A).</math>

In the case that '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup> is a [[topological group]] (that is, when ''n'' is 0, 1 or 3), spherical measure ''&sigma;''<sup>''n''</sup> coincides with (normalized) Haar measure on '''S'''<sup>''n''</sup>.

==Isoperimetric inequality==

There is an [[isoperimetric inequality]] for the sphere with its usual metric and spherical measure (see Ledoux &amp; Talagrand, chapter 1):

If ''A''&nbsp;&sube;&nbsp;'''S'''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup> is any Borel set and ''B''&sube;&nbsp;'''S'''<sup>''n''&minus;1</sup> is a ''&rho;''<sub>''n''</sub>-ball with the same ''&sigma;''<sup>''n''</sup>-measure as ''A'', then, for any ''r''&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;0,
:<math>\sigma^{n}(A_{r}) \geq \sigma^{n}(B_{r}),</math>
where ''A''<sub>''r''</sub> denotes the "inflation" of ''A'' by ''r'', i.e.
:<math>A_{r} := \{ x \in \mathbf{S}^{n} \mid \rho_{n}(x, A) \leq r \}.</math>
In particular, if ''&sigma;''<sup>''n''</sup>(''A'')&nbsp;≥&nbsp;{{sfrac|1|2}} and ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2, then
:<math>\sigma^{n}(A_{r}) \geq 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}} \, \exp \left( - \frac{(n - 1) r^{2}}{2} \right).</math>
